en: Śrī Rāma.
There is the servant of the servant of Śrī Rāma, who has made Gaṇeśa his own and is endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers;
likewise, there is Śāradā, whose nature is the fourfold speech.
Having bowed down to those two, who are the root of the creation of the universe and the infinite benefactor, I shall now proclaim the path of Rāma. || 1 ||
When your mind travels along the path of devotion to Rāma, then you will, by your very nature, attain that Śrī Hari; therefore,
you must not do that which is censured by people.
Action praised by men should be pursued with effort. || 2 ||
He who, at dawn, should contemplate Rāmacandra and then proclaim His virtues with melodious speech—
such a person of right conduct should never abandon this practice with a distracted mind.
In this world, he alone attains the state of being most blessed. || 3 ||
Quickly abandon the mental impressions that give rise to suffering; always cast off the sinful intent of the mind.
O mind, do not forsake the path of Dharma.
O mind, abide in this investigation which constitutes the very essence of reality.
The mind that delights in evil actions must certainly be abandoned; the mind whose resolve is truth alone must be cultivated.
Abandon the mental construction of sounds and other sense objects.
Alas, alas! You have fallen into this state by relying on these transformations. || 5 ||
O mind, let there be not even a trace of anger that brings affliction;
O mind, let there be no desire, the root of transformation;
O mind, do not embrace wicked pride.
Let there be no envy in your mind, nor let there be hypocrisy. || 6 ||

The mind should be fixed upon the noble paths; the mind of a base man possesses only the patience to endure insults. [O King,] you have [subdued] the mind with your cool and continuous streams of speech.
The minds of virtuous people should always be gratified. || 7 ||
O all you gods, undertake that action by which fame shall remain firm even at the fall of the body; for the mind,
when it embraces excellent virtues, becomes like sandalwood.
In every way, you must please virtuous people.
O mind, do not gather the forest belonging to another; for one whose intellect is intent on excessive self-interest, extreme sin remains here,
and its fruit— born of evil— is always to be experienced.
When there is no attainment of what is desired, then there is only suffering. || 9 ||
O Rāmacandra, may there always be love in your mind;
forcibly ward off the web of suffering residing within the heart. You must regard the suffering of the body as happiness.
May you always delight in the investigation of the nature of the self. || 10 ||
Who in this world is endowed with all happiness?
Reflect well with your mind and gradually determine this:
whatever karma was previously accumulated by your mind, [that alone you shall experience].
That very same thing is the object of experience here, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
O embodied one, let not the mind create an interval for the web of suffering; abandon grief and anxiety in every way. Then, through discernment, cast off the notion of a body.
Abide in Videha and partake in liberation; exert yourself! || 12 ||
O mind, speak this if it has been heard by you: in an instant, Rāvaṇa’s entire kingdom was utterly destroyed;
therefore, abandon this inauspicious tendency that bestows suffering.
Time comes by force, clinging to one's back. || 13 ||
This body was obtained by me through great merit,
yet at the time of death, it is taken away by Kṛtānta;
even the great indeed depart by the path of death.
Innumerable living beings have come into existence and perished. || 14 ||
O mind, behold those who dwell on the ground of death; though they speak of immortality, saying "I am indeed this,
I am thus," they cherish their own long life— alas!
In an instant, they abandon everything and depart. || 15 ||
Beholding a deceased kinsman, he grieves pointlessly for a moment, yet he too shall soon follow the path of death;
for his greed does not reach a state of peace.
Then he again enters into connection with a body. || 16 ||
People grieve pointlessly out of delusion;
that which is destined to happen will always happen in an instant.
Union with sons and others occurs through one's own past actions.
The person of small intellect suffers in vain when separated from that [object]. || 17 ||
Always fix your mind on the hope of Rāghava; do not mention any other man at all—
him whom the Purāṇas and the Vedas describe.
A man attains praise through the description of that [virtue]. || 18 ||
O mind, never abandon the truth of Brahman; O mind, do not entertain false thoughts under any circumstances.
O mind, always speak the truth through virtuous words.
Abandon the mind, which is non-existent, thinking "it is false. || 19 ||
Excessive exhaustion arises within the mother's womb;
therefore, the mind should not engage in that which leads to suffering.
The infant is cooked in the fire-pit of the digestive heat.
Then, with his head downward and feet upward, he became exceedingly exhausted. || 20 ||
O mind, quickly abandon that which bestows birth and death, which grants suffering, and which craves the acquisition of wealth and the company of loved ones;
for from this comes the unbearable agony of dwelling in the womb.
Therefore, establish a bond of affection with Rāghava. || 21 ||
This is beneficial for my mind; you must always perform this task today with diligence: the feet of Rāma, whose fame is renowned, must be served by you as the master of the son of the Wind.
He, the Lord of the three worlds, shall uplift all people.
O Manorāma, you should not speak anything else;
no one attains happiness through a mere proliferation of empty words,
for Time seizes life away in an instant.
Then, at the end of the body's life, who will liberate you? || 23 ||
Without service to Rāma, a person's exertion is entirely in vain, like the prattle of one who is asleep;
therefore, always utter the name of Hari with your speech.
O Great Sinful One, quickly destroy my egoism! || 24 ||
If you do not honor my words as being solely for your benefit, how will you ever attain the lotus feet of Rāma?
At the very moment of attaining happiness, only bliss arises.
From that, there is total destruction; nothing whatsoever remains stable. || 25 ||
Someone has made an effort to protect this body, yet in a mere moment that body has been carried away by time;
therefore, O mind, take refuge in Rāmacandra.
Release all anxiety from within regarding existence. || 26 ||
O mind, why do you fear out of dread of this worldly existence?
Abandon this thought and rely instead upon fortitude,
for the Lord Rāmacandra stands as your protector at your very head.
What indeed is this fear of yours of Kṛtānta, who holds a staff in his hand? || 27 ||
Seeing before him the Lord of the Wretched, the Master with bow in hand, even this Time itself trembles;
let my words be honored by people as the very truth.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 28 ||
This vow of Rāmacandra is indeed renowned: that the head of one who hates his devotee must certainly be struck,
by whom the city was led in an instant to the world of the gods.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 29 ||
Who on this earth is so devoid of intellect that he would look upon the Lord’s servant with a cruel eye,
when people throughout the three worlds sing his praises?
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 30 ||
He by whom the gods were liberated from great peril,
who is preeminent through his strength, majesty, and virtues,
and whom Ambikā and the wielder of the trident likewise remember.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 31 ||
By him, even Ahalyā, though her body had become stone, was rendered exceedingly pure through the touch of his feet;
at the description of his glory, even the Śruti fell silent.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 32 ||
The mind, the moon, the sun, the constellations, Mount Meru, and all else dwell instantly within its own nature;
by means of this [nature], its two servants have been brought to long life.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 33 ||
Equanimity belongs to no one else; it resides in the mind of the deluded person who lacks the realization of its true nature—
that which the ancients call the Protector of the Universe.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 34 ||
Whatever kind of disposition resides in one's own heart, the Lord dwells immediately in that very place in such a form;
He who holds a bow in His hand is the protector of those who have no other refuge.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 35 ||
Hari, the compassionate one, always remains in the presence of living beings upon seeing the fortitude of his own devotee;
he is indeed the bestower of happiness, bliss, and absolute liberation.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 36 ||
Just as the sun is the protector of the cakravāka bird, so too is the Lord the protector of his servant in times of distress;
thus is the greatness of devotion to Hari sung by the wise.
That Rāmacandra does not neglect his own devotee. || 37 ||
O you who are like the best of the Raghus, hear this single prayer of my mind;
remain steadfast and do not ever disregard these words of mine.
O Rāghava, let your mind dwell within me.
To him whom the Purāṇas and the Vedas describe,
and through whose company there may always be tranquility—
to him one should quickly surrender one's own fickleness.
Set your mind on dwelling with Rāghava.
The mind attains happiness wherever it may be; therefore, one should observe that with great care here,
having warded off evil thoughts through discernment.
Set your mind upon dwelling with Rāghava.
There is never any happiness in wandering about;
only fatigue arises, and nothing at all beneficial.
Having attained through discernment the awakening of profound bliss—
Set your mind upon dwelling with Rāghava.
Enough with further elaboration;
simply make your own mind Rāghava. Having heard his vow, "I am the protector of the distressed," [act accordingly].
O mind, dwell within your own true nature as a virtuous person. || 42 ||
"You must accept my one sincere word with your mind; you must by all means act for your own welfare.
Never, at any time, should anyone other than Rāma be spoken of here."
The true nature of the Self should always be meditated upon through profound contemplation. || 43 ||
If the mind is attached to the foolish, one should practice silence; if there is a fondness for talk, one should direct it toward Rāghava alone.
Abandoning that [worldly talk], one should go where Rāma is not present in the home.
For the sake of happiness, one should always dwell in the forest. || 44 ||
He whose concentration is broken by attachment,
whose egoism suddenly arises toward his own body,
and whose mind abandons Rāmacandra due to attachment— [such a person is lost].
What happiness can there be for men through association with that? 45.
O mind, that time has passed away deprived of Rāma; through the dullness of your intellect, you have destroyed your own life and vitality,
which is nothing but labor without service to Rāma.
He alone is truly capable here who is always a servant of Rāma.
Even a wise man who remains devoted to Hari, contemplating Him with his heart and beholding Him with his eyes,
and who practices spiritual discipline while possessed of love for His divine qualities;
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 47 ||
He who always applies his own body to the service of the gods, whose speech always utters the name of the True Lord,
and whose steadfastness is eternally rooted in his own supreme duty;
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 48 ||
He who always speaks the truth, walks by the right path,
and perceives the one God within the many,
shall worship Vāsudeva upon the destruction of his delusion.
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 49 ||
He whose mind is free from transformations such as desire and the like,
who is an ascetic, dispassionate, and himself a celibate student,
whose heart is ever peaceful and devoid of even a trace of darkness— [to him belongs this state].
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One.
He whose mind has cast out intoxication, envy, and the desire for self-interest, who feels no distress arising from worldly proliferation,
and who always speaks only words that are true and beneficial— [he is a sage].
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 51 ||
One should proceed by means of the restatement of the reflection on reality; being smeared with time, one is not defiled by faults such as hypocrisy and the like.
One performs the discourse on Brahman daily with the most excellent [practitioners].
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 52 ||
He who is always upright and beloved by all the world, who is ever and forever truthful and discerning,
never speaks a word that is false at any time.
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 53 ||
He who always dwells in the forest, even if young, whose mind is free from the impurity of conceptualization,
and whose firm conviction never departs from his heart— [he is a true ascetic].
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 54 ||
He from whose mind the deep-rooted and flourishing thirst for worldly existence has departed— thirst which takes the form of love for Hari—
and by whom the God of gods has been made his debtor through devotion; [he alone is truly liberated].
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One. || 55 ||
He who is compassionate and merciful, whose heart is tender toward people and filled with affection, and who is a protector of his servants—
he whose mind is not possessed by the torment of anger.
He is the blessed servant here of the Supreme One.
Through the chanting of Hari’s names and through worship,
a person attains constant blessedness in this world;
indifference toward worldly objects is the essence.
By that, there is always the pacification of the fluctuations of the mind. || 57 ||
Let there be no attachment of the mind to sounds and other objects; let desire for material things arise from past sins.
The Lord should be meditated upon with perfectly desireless devotion.
Even a mere trace of conceptual construction must be swiftly abandoned. || 58 ||
A person who conceptualizes a mental construction approaches Rāma, the Lord, for millions of eons— yet not at all, not at all—
if that person, held by their mind, is not Rāma himself.
How could there be any connection with great affection for Rāma in him? || 59 ||
Rāmacandra is the mind, the treasure-trove, the wish-fulfilling cow, the celestial tree, and the jewel that grants desired objects;
for by his power alone exists the reality of everything.
No one in the world attains equality with him. || 60 ||
Suffering persists in the mind of one who, though always distressed, relies upon the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) while engaging in disputes with virtuous people.
Then he experiences great internal anguish. || 61 ||
Indeed, for such a person, even the interruption of profound meditation (nididhyāsana) would arise forcibly as a state of grief and torment;
through the perception of duality, the destruction of blissful joy would occur.
Alas, all mental determination has vanished! || 62 ||
Just as the Lord of the Wish-Fulfilling Cow [requests] curd, so too does the knower of the Self have a fondness for debate; he is like one who,
having abandoned the wish-fulfilling gem, seeks fragments of glass.
One should entreat him; who would not grant those [boons] to him? || 63 ||
The intellect of a deluded man is not firm; in the mind of one agitated by excessive desire, there is no Rāma.
When great gain occurs, his mind becomes disturbed.
One who is excessively attached to sensual enjoyments falls into wretchedness.
Through lack of devotion to Hari, let there be no life;
in extreme folly, there would be only constant misery upon misery.
Offer your mind to Rāmacandra with the yoga of love.
May you have no desire for wealth and such things during the intervals [of meditation]. || 65 ||
This cycle of existence is essence-less and exceedingly terrible;
therefore, O mind, seek out the virtuous, for that alone is the truth.
If you were to consume poison, how could there be any happiness for you?
Therefore, you should always contemplate Rāmacandra.
He who is dark as a rain-cloud, endowed with extreme beauty, profound, exceedingly steadfast, and full of majesty;
he who is a partisan for his devotee in times of distress.
That Rāma is to be meditated upon in the heart at dawn. || 67 ||
Rāghava, with bow in hand, is superior in strength; even the formidable Kāla himself fears him—
what then can be said of a wretched mortal?
At dawn, Rāghava should be meditated upon with the heart. || 68 ||
He who brings happiness and joy and wards off fear should indeed be served in this world through the practice of love,
having abandoned the notion of misconduct through discernment.
At dawn, Rāghava should be meditated upon with the heart. || 69 ||
O mind, praise Hari, the fulfiller of desires;
then you shall never again be oppressed by the snares of suffering. You must quickly abandon pride and sloth.
At dawn, Rāghava should be meditated upon with the heart. || 70 ||
By the chanting of which there is the destruction of great faults,
by the chanting of which a person attains a good state,
and by the chanting of which there may be an increase of merit.
That Rāma is to be meditated upon in the heart at dawn. || 71 ||
There would be no expenditure of one's own wealth whatsoever in the utterance of the name of Rāma; rather,
through it, the destruction of the enemy that is saṃsāra occurs.
That Rāma is to be meditated upon in the heart at dawn. || 72 ||
Great suffering arises from corporal punishment, but there is no suffering at all in the chanting of His name—
he who is the God of gods, whom Śiva himself contemplates.
That Rāma is to be meditated upon in the heart at dawn. || 73 ||
In practices preceded by austerity, there is physical hardship; likewise, charity, the fulfillment of vows, and other rites require wealth alone.
He who is always compassionate toward miserable living beings—[he is truly a practitioner].
At dawn, Rāghava should be meditated upon with the heart. || 74 ||
Among the means for achieving mental mastery, this alone is praised; if you do not believe this, let the virtuous determine it for you.
This useless doubt must indeed be abandoned, as it brings about one's end.
At dawn, Rāghava is to be meditated upon with the heart. || 75 ||
Neither yoga, nor dharma, nor ritual action, nor enjoyment, nor renunciation— not even one of these— can be complete without it;
place your faith in the chanting of the Name of the Lord.
At dawn, Rāghava should be meditated upon with the heart. || 76 ||
One who has faith in the congregational chanting of Hari’s name,
who recites the name of Rāma free from dualities,
and who performs the service of Hari, shall become free from desire.
And at that time, one should perceive one's own true nature everywhere. || 77 ||
Alas! That base person who would never have a mind of trust in Rāma shall always be a partaker of suffering;
yet, while Rāmacandra, the bestower of liberation, remains present—
The concern for the body and the cycle of existence is in vain for one of small intellect. || 78 ||
Place within your heart the purifying contemplation of Rāghava; let there be no anxiety regarding worldly existence,
for *bhava* (worldly becoming) ever causes the living soul to wander.
The preservation of a non-existent object is indeed useless. || 79 ||
Take refuge this very day in the heart-dwelling Lord Śrīśamīśa and cross over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to traverse;
you must abandon this insatiable desire that is so hard to bear.
A harsh and envious person must certainly be punished in every way. || 80 ||
O mind, do not abandon the name of the Lord of Śrī due to stinginess;
let this constant meditation upon it be yours with the utmost devotion. O mind, the supreme name of Rāma is your means of attainment!
And there is nothing at all equal to this in the world. || 81 ||
There are many other names equal to this one,
yet this wretched commoner does not know them due to his lack of fortune;
this poison-destroying [mantra] was realized by the Lord of Pārvatī.
What talk can there be here of a mere human being, a servant? || 82 ||
Constantly meditating on Rāma, the enemy of Smara, the Lord joined by Umā sings while bound by love,
endowed with the power of firm detachment.
He always dwells in happiness, filled with confidence in Rāma. || 83 ||
Even Śiva, the Lord who resides upon the head of Viṭṭhala, was absorbed in meditation on Him; why then are you not?
For even Nīlakaṇṭha attained peace thereby.
That Rāma indeed shall liberate a man from the God of Death.
One should worship Rāghava, the cause of rest for yogis; Maheśa repeats his names along with Gaurī,
and Śaṅkara himself became an ascetic and peaceful through him.
For in the end, O Rāma, this alone shall be the bestower of liberation. || 85 ||
He in whose mouth is Rāma possesses constant happiness; he remains forever immersed in the form of eternal bliss.
Without Rāma, there is only doubt and distress elsewhere.
One's own name is indeed one's abode, and it removes all sorrow.
He in whose mouth Rāma resides has no desire in his heart,
nor shall there be a loss of that fortitude in times of distress; for, by means of the yoga of devotion to Hari, he has completely conquered desire.
That son of the Wind, a celibate student, became blessed. || 87 ||
The name of Rāma is exceedingly supreme, beautiful, concise in syllables, priceless, easily attainable, and beneficial;
it destroys worldly existence for those who chant it.
That very same state is here the form of liberation for men. || 88 ||
One should always utter the name of Rāma at the beginning of a meal; thereafter, during the eating, it should be proclaimed with reverence.
In this manner, one should utter the meritorious name with every morsel.
Then Śrī Hari is attained by His very nature. || 89 ||
For one who is always devoid of the Name, there is terrible ruin;
that birth is worthless for which there is no reverence for the Name.
The Name of Hari is the supreme good in the Vedas and the scriptures.
The supreme syllable has indeed been proclaimed through the words of Vyāsa. || 90 ||
O Ramacandra, you must not remain indifferent;
one should chant the name of Hari with devotion.
There is no expense whatsoever in chanting the name of Rama.
Then one should proclaim the name of the Lord of Jānakī.
When Rāma’s name is proclaimed with reverence, the faults residing within one's own heart depart far away;
Hari remains delighted upon hearing his glory.
Therefore, the illustrious Śiva is solely intent upon the name of Rāma. || 92 ||
He who is the Lord, the giver of food at his own will even unto insects,
whose concern for living beings is ever-present in his heart—
even though the chanting of His name is so easily accessible, you [remain indifferent].
The mind is indeed failing; tell me quickly, what is that? 93.
That Lord who was capable of incinerating the three worlds when enraged attained tranquility through the chanting of whose name;
and by whom the Mother of the Universe, Śivā, is recited with devotion.
That alone should be proclaimed here by all people. || 94 ||
The evil-doer Ajāmila attained liberation merely by chanting the name of his son, "Nārāyaṇa";
likewise, the harlot attained it by calling out to Śuka as "Rāghava."
He attained great renown, well-established in the Purāṇas. || 95 ||
The supreme devotee named Prahlāda, though born into the lineage of the Daityas, constantly chanted the Name;
his wicked-souled father could not endure that at all.
On this earth, he did not even utter the name of Rāma.
If Rāma did not speak thus, how could there be liberation for him?
Under the sway of egoism, he would undergo suffering in vain;
therefore, upon the destruction of the body, he would experience great misery.
Therefore, say "Rāma, Rāma" constantly! || 97 ||
It is clear that stones have been crossed by the name of Rāma; here, many dull-witted men have been made to cross over.
Yet, one who is always of a doubting nature remains [behind] due to its power.
He who does not even mutter [the mantra] is a man whose very form is sin. || 98 ||
For in this world, Vārāṇasī is a land of merit,
where people who go there deliver their ancestors; there,
the moon-crested Lord eternally chants the name of Rāma.
He remained there for the purpose of awakening living beings. || 99 ||
It is not possible for men to perform actions correctly; even when a religious duty has been performed, there is no attainment of merit,
for there is no compassion toward all living beings in their hearts.
Alas, the priceless name of Hari is not in our mouths! 100.
Time does not punish one for whom the Name is dear;
yet through conceptualization and false reasoning, one's destination may be hellish.
Therefore, the Name should be recited with devotion.
From that, the destruction of defects arises by its very nature. || 101 ||
Having accepted humility as their very nature,
the virtuous should satisfy the minds [of others] with that;
and having employed their own bodies for the benefit of the world, they should remain so.
One should worship the Lord with form through the joy of non-birth. || 102 ||
May there be delight in the virtues of Hari during the chanting of His glories;
may there be no sense of "I" in the realization of the Supreme Brahman;
and likewise, may there be no attachment to the wealth of others or to the beloved of another.
Deeply rooted conceit must indeed be abandoned. || 103 ||
He whose conduct does not accord with what he speaks is deluded and incurs shame thereby; for him,
there is only the mind, while his speech is mere confusion.
How could that fool ever attain the God of gods?
Abandoning your own impure actions due to a lack of discernment,
perform pure actions with devotion;
act exactly as you speak.
Abandon the mental construction that bestows cyclic existence. || 105 ||
Having performed his daily duties such as the twilight prayers, one should, through discernment, steady the mind that has strayed from the Self;
he for whom compassion toward all beings has fully increased—
Through a state of constant devotion, he attains peace. || 106 ||
One should never allow the mind to become provoked to anger;
rather, direct the mind toward the company of the virtuous. Always abandon attachment to wicked people.
Therefore, it is true that you shall obtain liberation through that [mind]. || 107 ||
Through constant association with the virtuous, the minds of men shall always be free from corruption and possess devotion to the Lord;
let there be no boastful talk for you unless it is accompanied by righteous action.
That in which there is no loss of the argument is accepted as a valid discourse. || 108 ||
Cavil should always be avoided here by all who seek the highest happiness; instead, one should engage in excellent debate.
Only a well-conducted discussion removes sorrow in this world.
That which results in the defeat of the debate is accepted as a "concordant statement" (saṃvāda). || 109 ||
That which destroys false discourse is indeed true discourse; through discernment, pride itself must be conquered,
for it is the sense of "I" that creates distortions in debate.
That in which there is no loss of the argument is accepted as a valid discussion (saṃvāda). || 110 ||
This speech of truth has been uttered for your very benefit;
therefore, having reflected upon it for your own welfare, act accordingly here.
For your benefit alone, you must abandon the mindset of a heretic.
That in which there is no loss of the argument is accepted as a valid discussion. || 111 ||
The birth of the speaker has passed away, as has that of the listener; yet the dispute alone remains unappeased among people.
This doubt born of dispute creates hypocrisy.
That in which there is no loss of the argument is accepted as a valid discussion. || 112 ||
The wise, intoxicated by debate, have forgotten what is beneficial;
through the power of egoism, they have become like demons.
Without the Supreme Lord, there is no one who is truly wise.
Therefore, O mind, abandon your own egoism. || 113 ||
In instructing others, there is no expense at all;
rather, with every passing moment, the force of one's pride increases. Fie upon mere eloquence in speech without corresponding action!
Therefore, resolve this with your mind through every means with great reverence. || 114 ||
One should not converse with that man who is devoted to disputation; rather, through discernment, even the slightest trace of egoism must be abandoned by men.
Whatever one speaks, that alone one should practice in every way.
One whose actions are purified should proceed by way of devotion. || 115 ||
Viṣṇu himself took upon himself the suffering of dwelling in the womb born of the sage’s curse for Ambarīṣa,
and Śiva gave Upamanyu the ocean of milk.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.

Having observed Dhruva, who was thus possessed of wretchedness, and having looked upon him with compassion as he was supremely intent on meditation, He made him immovable in the host of stars— him [I salute].
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
The lordly elephant, his limbs exhausted, being seized by the foot by a fierce crocodile in the lake, remembered Viṣṇu alone;
Hari, arriving at that very moment, liberated him.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee. || 118 ||
The twice-born Ajāmila, though a doer of evil deeds, attained liberation at the time of his death by uttering the name of his son;
for the wielder of the discus is the refuge of the helpless.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee. || 119 ||
For the benefit of the Creator, he became a fish;
in the form of a tortoise, he bore the immovable earth upon his back. Indeed, to protect his own devotees, he has resorted to lowly births.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
He who assumed the fierce form of Nṛsiṃha for the sake of protecting the great devotee Prahlāda—
no one at all is capable of approaching His presence.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
When Vajrapāṇi indeed begged for mercy,
then Cakrapāṇi himself became Vāmana;
likewise, he who was Bhārgava became so for the sake of the twice-born.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
Out of partiality for Ahalyā and Satī, he resorted to the forest and even sought to liberate the gods from bondage;
he was the one who struck down the banner of his enemy Rāvaṇa.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
In ancient times, for the sake of Draupadī’s pleasure, the God of gods himself appeared there at that very moment;
likewise, he became Maunibuddha in the Kali age.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
In the Kali age, he alone shall manifest as Kalki specifically to protect his own devoted followers who are without a protector;
regarding the proclamation of his qualities, even the Veda has attained silence.
That God of gods does not neglect his own devotee.
Indeed, he by whom many playful incarnations were previously assumed upon the earth for the sake of favoring humanity—
he who does not serve him is truly a great sinner.
He was evil-minded, possessed of wicked intellect, and had the form of a Cāṇḍāla. || 126 ||
He is blessed who is pacified by the sound of Hari’s name;
likewise, having heard His story, he becomes absorbed therein,
and his own evil intellect is destroyed through his self-awakening.
He whose mental impressions have dissolved into Rāma. || 127 ||
Let your mental impressions be fixed upon Vāsudeva; let there be no desire for attachment to worldly objects. You should not engage in vain mental constructions at all.
O noble mind! Delight in the company of the virtuous. || 128 ||
The mind [is directed] toward attaining a good rebirth through association with the virtuous;
from that, the evil intellect of the wicked perishes,
for he realizes that the Lord of Love is the agitator of the mind.
The wise should exert effort toward the state of selflessness.
O mind, let there be no doubt in you regarding Rāma; let your heart always remain one whose resolve is ever true.
And forever renounce all idle chatter in this world.
Worship the Beloved of Ramā with single-minded devotion. || 130 ||
Indeed, Rāma alone is to be served by people in this world; he is one in speech and likewise one in his arrow,
and his life-story is that which uplifts all beings.
That lord of Sītā is to be served first through discernment. || 131 ||
Only for one who speaks or acts after having reflected does the fever of suffering subside through that association;
there is nothing whatsoever to be said without reflection.
And one must always proceed only upon the path of the righteous. || 132 ||
Dispassion, devotion, the yoga of discernment, and a firm, constant self-awareness within the heart—
seeing and touching such a person is always meritorious.
Likewise, such a statement is destructive of doubt. || 133 ||
He who possesses no pride, who is ever free from passion, endowed with patience and tranquility, and skillful in compassion;
in whom there is neither agitation nor greed, nor even dejection.
Therein, the state of being a lord of yogis is attained directly. || 134 ||
One should cultivate association with the virtuous, for through it even the mind of the wicked attains purity;
thus one gains true goodness, right understanding, and the path of the righteous.
From that, one attains fearlessness from the formidable and terrible Time. || 135 ||
Indeed, this infinite universe is always filled with fear, whereas the virtuous are truly fearless;
for one who is bowed down before that [Reality], there occurs the cessation of duality.
Fear of the mind has been destroyed for him in every respect. || 136 ||
Indeed, the best have departed after awakening the living soul here; yet, alas, this living soul still remains here,
for its egoism and karma do not undergo dissolution.
He does not find peace through the sense of "I-ness. || 137 ||
Due to delusion, for whom the mass of consciousness became hidden, death manifested as the giver of birth and poverty;
he in whom the notion of the body being the self has not dissolved here.
He does not find peace through the notion of "I. || 138 ||
Alas, the unfortunate person does not know the reality of the Self, which is all-pervading; instead, they consider the visible world to be insentient.
Furthermore, one who lacks faith possesses not even a trace of merit.
One does not find bliss through the sense of "I-ness. || 139 ||
One's own true nature is not attained due to one's own negligence;
for attachment to the qualities (guṇas) is here the cause of suffering,
as long as one does not abide in a state that transcends the qualities.
The treasure does not exist at all as long as there is egoism.
Now, there exists one who knows Brahman; his service and his pair of feet are likewise worthy of worship.
Without the ointment of the True Guru, that [Brahman] cannot be known.
This treasure cannot be attained through the "I-ness" of the mind. || 141 ||
As long as that [delusion] does not come to an end, and as long as the destruction of doubt has not occurred for the utterly deluded one,
so long does the sense of "I" not depart.
That is not found by force, nor is it obtained. || 142 ||
Under the sway of ignorance, the man of deluded intellect does not attain his own welfare, which has been forgotten through error;
just as one who, without examination, accepts what is impure.
That coin is not for the purpose of purchasing the object one desires.
What indeed is the truth regarding the mind in this world? You must investigate that with earnestness;
by doing so, you will experience the reality of Brahman.
Then, the delusion born of non-origination comes to an end. || 144 ||

The multitude of living beings always arises from the thought of the visible world; when one is bowed down by egoism, this [world] appears. Therefore, through discernment, one should always cultivate one’s own true nature.
For indeed, in the root of Brahman, there is neither birth nor death. || 145 ||
That which is not within the range of perception could never arise spontaneously; and that which arises would perish in time,
because everything perishes and nothing is stable.
The mind, which is infinite being and consciousness, is to be thoroughly sought. || 146 ||
It is neither to be broken, nor cut, nor moved, nor subject to fall; it stands everywhere as the "I-sense" (ahaṃtā) and is not an object of cognition.
For that which is of a single nature, duality is simply impossible.
The mind, which is infinite existence and consciousness, is to be thoroughly sought. || 147 ||

Even regarding that which is of the nature of the Self-Existent (Svayambhū) and the like, the Veda attained silence in its description because it is immutable; that form is to be attained through discernment.
The mind, which is infinite existence and consciousness, is to be thoroughly sought. || 148 ||
That which cannot be perceived by the physical eye in this world,
yet can be beheld by the eye of wisdom in this very world— that vision, upon seeing which, the act of looking itself dissolves.
The mind is to be sought after; it is the form of eternal bliss. || 149 ||
It is neither yellow, nor white, nor dark; it is neither manifest nor of unmanifest form, nor blue.
Yet, when trust is fully placed in the Reliable One, it bestows liberation here.
The mind is to be sought after; it is the form of eternal bliss. || 150 ||
By repeatedly reflecting upon the reality that is to be known,
by awakening the mind that is to be awakened, and by realizing that which is to be realized,
all success is attained through supreme association with virtuous people.
A firm resolve arises from that state of passion. || 151 ||
When the enumeration of the principles and the yoga of skillfulness have been accomplished,
the awakening to the Supreme Brahman is indeed inevitable;
however, the mind, which is the very essence, remains far from the truth.
For that is indeed one alone and without a second within all things. || 152 ||

There is no state of meditative absorption through the senses or the body when they are deprived [of their objects], nor through the metaphysical principles (tattvas), nor through passionate outcries;
it is not attained through yogas, nor through sacrifices, nor through renunciation or enjoyment.
But that [state] would clearly arise from association with virtuous people. || 153 ||
Likewise, through the exposition of the five groups [of mantras] based on the realization of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya),
there is indeed the pointing out of the direction of the Supreme Brahman;
this is for the purpose of beholding the Moon on the second day.
Just as they point out the branches of a tree with their fingers. || 154 ||
That which is not seen in the world, when observed and scrutinized, becomes clear at that very moment;
yet it cannot be grasped in the hand, even with great effort.
But that which exists everywhere is not [directly] cognizable. || 155 ||
He who says, "I am the one who knows Brahman," is himself incapable of investigating that which is inconceivable in this world;
for that [notion] arises from the power of egoism, and thus it is not [realized] by the deluded.
When that is perceived, who is there distinct from it? || 156 ||
There is great exhaustion in surveying numerous treatises, yet therein lies no certainty regarding unity;
for the contradiction arising from the scriptures is inherently disputatious.
On the contrary, the intellect dissolves into the awakening of the Self. || 157 ||
The Vedas, the six systems of philosophy, as well as the Dharmaśāstras—
even the thousand-faced Śeṣanāga himself—
is utterly incapable of describing them in their entirety.
Therefore, you must abandon the pride of mental conceit. || 158 ||
If a fly consisting of the sense of "I" (ahantā) has been swallowed, how could there be any relish in the food for that man?
For as long as that "I-ness" residing in the heart does not depart.
Food is not well-digested as long as [the previous meal] has not been digested. || 159 ||
O mind, let there be no thought that causes weariness in debate; let there be no delight in duality that causes anger.
O mind, remain so until the end of this sense of "I."
For you are not worthy of giving gifts to others. || 160 ||
When egoism arises, all suffering is born;
news emerging from the mouth [of the ego] is indeed in vain.
When egoism is destroyed, you shall find happiness everywhere.
O mind, contemplate that very egoism yourself.
Even in solitude, by the force of egoism, a person falls into unrighteousness; through unrighteousness, he attains praise in the world,
yet in his heart he perceives his own state of hypocrisy.
His intellect abandons other means of valid cognition. || 162 ||

He whose firm conviction is that the notion of the body being the self is utterly alien to the true Self has indeed departed; therefore, one must firmly maintain the realization of the Self, abandoning that notion of the body as the self.
One should always cultivate association with virtuous people. || 163||
The dualistic cognition imagined by the mind should be abandoned; the conception of non-duality should be held firmly in the heart.
Upon abiding in one's true nature, even that [conception] shall vanish from within the heart.
One should always cultivate the company of virtuous people. || 164 ||
For through the contemplation of one's own body and so forth within the realm of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the mind increases and greed grows within oneself;
therefore, through devotion to the Lord of Śrī, one should strive for liberation.
For that purpose, one should always cultivate the company of the virtuous. || 165 ||
This expansion of egoism— consisting of the body, beloved ones, sons, friends, and so forth— is born of delusion;
therefore, one should cast off this delusion of "I," which is the cause of birth.
For that purpose, one should always cultivate the company of the virtuous. || 166 ||
A firm resolve must be made for the eternal alone; the mind's doubt arising from the words of a servant should be cast aside,
so that there may be the meaningfulness of birth at every single moment.
For that purpose, one should always cultivate the company of the virtuous. || 167 ||
That virtuous person makes his own mental state tranquil;
he does not fall into wretchedness by resorting to evil desires,
for the notion that the body is the self is indeed the condition that causes such increase.
How could that [craving] obstruct the virtuous one's dispassion? || 168 ||
One should indeed approach the virtuous for the sake of infinite awakening;
one should cast off this expansion of egoism.
For having attained transcendence of the qualities (guṇātītatā), the Infinite is to be contemplated.
One should never, in this world, entertain the notion that the body is the self. || 169 ||

One should abandon the notion of the body being the self through the realization of the Self; through discernment, one should practice union with the Reality. A mental modification in the form of consciousness should not be cultivated as something external.
Therefore, that should always be sought after. || 170 ||
That which is a well-guarded, existing entity, being the very essence, is merely within the range of the eye and visible;
yet this [other] is invisible, appearing as the absence of qualities.
Due to the power of egoism, it is not perceived even with effort. || 171 ||
Conceptualization regarding objects is indeed manifest; that by which Brahman is differentiated is ignorance (avidyā), while that by which it is realized is true knowledge (suvijñā).
For in the primordial aeon, that Māyā became twofold.
Through discernment, she becomes dissolved in the nature of the Self. || 172 ||
For when the Rāhu of egoism arises within the sky of consciousness,
the space of consciousness is indeed seen to be obscured;
like a night of darkness, there occurs even a confusion of the directions.
Through discernment and inquiry, that [reality] may be directly realized. || 173 ||
That which cannot be perceived even with effort by the eye,
and by consuming which there is no protection from existence—
yet that which bestows inexhaustible liberation is itself inexhaustible.
The compassionate one takes the side of his own devotee. || 174 ||
Fate indeed writes what is destined to be upon the forehead of all;
who else is the scribe upon that forehead?
Even Hara, the destroyer of all at the time of the end, is subject to it.
But by what is Śaṅkara himself consumed at the end? || 175 ||
By whom those twelve Āditya gods, as well as countless Śakras and Rudras, were created—
that god, though sought after, is not found.
It is not understood what kind [of thing] it is, nor who is the principal one. || 176 ||
The God of gods cannot be divided, nor can he be broken; he cannot be moved, nor bent, nor is he ever like one who is wretched.
He is not of a form that can be given away, nor is he within the range of the physical eye.
Though all-pervading, he does not manifest through the sense of "I. || 177 ||
Whoever is dear to someone, that person is worthy of worship for him as a god;
yet no one truly knows the God of gods.
Indeed, infinite gods dwell upon this earth.
Where there is delight, there alone exists that excellent devotion.
From whom these three worlds were born— that best of gods no one here can describe;
that most excellent god remains well-concealed within the world.
Without a true guru, it can never be seen. || 179 ||
There are many millions on earth who remain in a state of heaviness,
capable in numerous mantras and tantras,
yet always desiring their own pleasure and acting as authors of stories and songs.
They merely cause delusion for men and do not bestow liberation. || 180 ||
He is indeed neither a deceiver, nor a practitioner of malevolent magic, nor one who is wealthy, nor a slanderer, nor envious, nor devoid of devotion;
he causes no affliction through association with him, nor does he steal his wealth.
But that awakening to Brahman which occurs within the world is the true one. || 181 ||
A lustful man might speak of dispassion with his heart,
yet without that corresponding action, his eloquence is in vain;
for a person's conduct is exactly as their speech describes it.
The mind must be certain that he alone is the true guru. 182.
One who is discerning, dispassionate, devoted, compassionate, wise, and patient; one who is disciplined in yoga, highly skillful, powerful, clever, and learned.
Through association with him, there may be the attainment of meditative concentration. || 183 ||
That which is unborn and likewise that which is yet to come— whatever indeed is produced by the words of the virtuous,
and that which is truly inexpressible, is nevertheless expressed.
The mind must seek out that which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
One should diligently become absorbed in the form of Rāma; the state beyond fear is certain within one's own true nature,
which can never be found here even when sought.
That which is always one cannot possess differentiation within it. || 185 ||
O noble-minded one, Rāghava is always present within the vicinity of your mind; therefore, seek the truth,
for your union with Rāghava remains unbroken.
Cast out that sense of "I" from within yourself.
The entire equality of the elements between the mind and the cosmic egg is indeed this Brahman; within the form of Brahman, nothing exists as such.
Whatever appears to the mind does not exist as a reality.
Having abandoned attachment, one should abide in happiness. || 187 ||
Having severed the noose of "I-ness" with the weapons of discernment, one should, out of devotion, adopt the state of being bodiless (videha-sthiti);
having abandoned all that is censurable through the power of dispassion.
Having abandoned attachment, one should abide in happiness. || 188 ||
The God who created the earth and other elements is to be beheld;
by beholding Him, liberation is attained immediately.
Endowed with attributes, yet devoid of attributes, He is to be served.
Having abandoned attachment, one should abide in happiness. || 189 ||
He is neither the performer of our actions nor the sustainer of our creation; he is higher than the highest, untainted by the process of phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*).
He is indeed beyond all conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), yet he is to be served through conceptual construction itself.
Having abandoned attachment, one should remain here in happiness. || 190||
He for whom the certainty of the notion that the body is the self has not perished would remain subject to rebirth even at the end of an aeon;
no one knows the Supreme Brahman through the sense of "I-ness."
One does not abandon the emptiness born of the mind. || 191 ||
That true nature of the Supreme Being, which is stable and devoid of mental contact, should indeed be contemplated as non-different from oneself;
for there can be no analogy whatsoever suitable for it.
In that state, non-attachment is not truly attached. || 192 ||
The Supreme Lord is neither spread out nor unspread out;
He is described by us through the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas. He is neither invisible nor visible, nor is He the witness of those two.
Even the Śruti does not know its end.
Then the practitioner respectfully asked: "Who is this preeminent deity, the Guru, who dwells within the heart? Of what nature is he?
And where does he reside after casting off the body?"
Where is a place suitable for him to dwell again?
Thus he spoke: "Know that the Divine indeed dwells within the heart; like the sky, it is eternally all-pervasive yet unattached.
It neither goes forth nor does it ever come."
Without that, there is no ground at all that is empty.
Not even a speck of dust from the delusions of the sky appears empty when the Lord of the Raghus is present;
for anyone who has set out to behold Him finds that very space filled with Him.
It goes to dissolution, both unperceived and perceived; and that which was perceived becomes dissolved.
Like the sky, that pervasive form of Rāma, when meditated upon with the heart, becomes the cause for the destruction of worldly existence;
through the realization of it, the notion of a body dissolves.
Even when well-beheld, there is no satisfaction according to one's desire. || 197 ||
Just as this sky stands pervading the entire universe, so it is with Rāma; there is no equality whatsoever between them.
For Rāma, by his very nature, is indeed non-dual.
For that purpose, the word "pervasive" (vyāpaka) is indeed redundant. || 198 ||
That ancient reality which is extended everywhere, whose true nature not even a trace of logic can penetrate,
yet which is hidden and supreme— may it quickly become easy to understand.
On account of his majesty, he was peerless among teachers. || 199 ||
But when one's own nature arises through this yoga,
all latent witness-hood becomes manifest therein; the mind transcends the levels (unmanī), and speech immediately becomes stilled.
He alone is himself the vision of Rāma, which [pervades] everywhere.
When self-realization occurs, nothing second ever appears;
indeed, not even a trace of duality remains in the mind.
Through many successions of births, one attains the realization of one's true nature.
When abiding in the state beyond the body (videha), there is the complete relinquishing of all bodily forms. || 201 ||
That which is most secret has indeed been attained by you; therefore, you must make it public, yet you must exert effort in its protection.
This should always be heard for the sake of firm conviction.
For through association with the virtuous, the mind indeed attains blessedness.
Having completely renounced all attachments, one should always respectfully cultivate the company of the virtuous from afar;
for through association with the good, the destruction of great suffering occurs.
Without that means, there is the attainment of the true path. || 203 ||
Association with the virtuous removes all attachments from the mind; this very association grants liberation at that very moment. This [association] swiftly liberates those who practice it.
This mind is in every respect capable of destroying duality. || 204 ||
Upon hearing the awakening of the mind, the dull-witted defects depart and attain a state of unfitness for further activity;
from that, one attains the power of discernment and dispassion.
Liberation arises from that through reliance on the words of the servant. || 205 ||
Victory, victory to you, O capable hero of Rādhā!
Then, in the year measured by the moon (one) marked by the clouds (zero) of virtues (three)— that is, 301— in the bright fortnight of Caitra, on the ninth day, a Sunday,
while the sun was scorching, he, standing on its bank, composed this *Manobodha*.
The servant of the guru Rāmadāsa has composed [this].
However, it is not fitting for us to publish this entire work again with its true meaning revealed, as it would be flawed;
therefore, [this was done] by one who was urged by the venerable Samarthas.
May this entire work, thoroughly purified, be for your delight.
Again and again, I bow to Śrī Rāma, the remover of calamities, the bestower of all prosperity, and the delight of the world.
Victory to Śrī Rāma! Victory to Rāma! Victory, victory to Rāma!
